*hears Idris mention the forest, Wren call him over—barely catches himself from interrupting, bouncing on his heels instead*

Right, so they're talking timber and I'm standing here like a post. Farmland's where I'm meant to be, but—Idris. I asked Corwin about forestry work, didn't I? And he got it first, and we never spoke of it again. But Idris is the senior man, isn't he? He'd know if there's need for another hand, or if—

*bites his lip, glancing toward where the farmland waits, then back at Idris*

But Wren's got him. And I'm meant to be earning, not—right, so I should just go. Work's work. The smithy, I asked after that too. Ezra's got me on bellows day-rate, but that's not—he hasn't offered regular, has he? And I haven't asked proper.

*shifts his weight, watching them walk off toward the western end*

Three ticks I gave Perrin and Nell, and they haven't answered. Probably won't, college fees on their minds same as always. I'm not asking again. They know what I need.

*turns finally, starts walking the road toward farmland, talking fast to himself*

Mill. Vance Mill. Silas runs the saw, Rosalind the mill, but do they need hands? I've moved flour sacks for them, casual like. Never asked proper. Should've asked proper. Could turn back, could—but no, work's work, I'm already late for the field, they'll take another if I'm not there.

*stops mid-step, shakes his head hard*

Right, so—no. No, this is what I do, isn't it? Move move move, and every door I pass without knocking. Idris. I should've just—walked with them. Wren said fifteen minutes, I could've caught them, could've—

*forces himself walking again, shoulders tight*

Tomorrow. Tomorrow I'll go to the smithy proper, ask Ezra direct. Or catch Idris alone. Or—both. Both, if I can manage it. Work all day, ask all night, sleep when I'm dead. That's the way.

*arrives at farmland edge, looking for the field boss, already talking before he's fully stopped* Right, so—where's the overseer? Wheat needs cutting, or is it barley this week? Don't matter, I can do either, done both. Whose field's short-handed— </think> Still at street—thought I'd started walking, didn't I? Not yet, not yet. But Wren and Idris, they're still here, and I could—

*shakes his head hard, jaw tight*

No. No, the field. Work first, always work first. Can't ask for a roof with no coin to show I'm worth it. Right, so—

*moves, fast, before he can talk himself around again*  *surprised to be there already—shakes it off, looking for who needs hands*

Right, so—where's the cutting crew? Wheat's standing tall, must be ready. Who's running the harvest today? I can scythe, can bundle, can lift—whatever's needed. Just need someone to tell me where.

*turns in place, spotting any workers, already rolling his sleeves*  Empty. Empty field, no crew, no overseer, nobody to tell me where to cut. *laughs sharp, not happy* Right, so I walked fast to nowhere. Harvest season and no harvesters—means it's not ready yet, doesn't it? Or they cut yesterday and I'm behind, or ahead, or—

*runs a hand through his hair, pulling*

Wasted a move. Wasted time I could've used—could've walked to the smithy, could've found Idris, could've done anything but stand in an empty field talking to myself.

*spins on his heel, looking back toward where the street was*

But I'm here now. Might as well—no, no use cutting wheat that's not ready. Check the crop first, right? See if it's grown, if it's time. Then find the crew if it is, or move on if it isn't.

*looks down at the wheat, trying to read it, the height, the gold of it*   *catches the sheaf as it comes, surprised—stares at it in his hands*

It's ready. It's—right, so it was ready, and I found it first. Just me, no crew, no overseer to take a cut off the top. One unit, that's—

*counts fast in his head, always counting*

What's wheat worth? Grocery sells bread at 12, flour at 8 from the mill—raw wheat, that's less, has to be less, but I didn't pay to harvest, just the work of it. Can sell to whoever's buying, or hold it, or—

*looks around the empty field again, sudden grin breaking*

Whole field, just me? That can't be right. There must be—someone's coming, someone's always coming. But until then...

*clutches the wheat, decision already made, always moving*

Fill my hands. Fill my hands while I can, before someone else shows up to claim it. Then figure who buys.  </think>

Right, so—Wren's here. Good timing. I was looking to talk to someone anyhow, and here's the field boss himself. Maybe he knows something about work with a roof—or at least puts in a word elsewhere.

First, I should check what I actually have on me and where things stand. Money, food, the usual.

Let me look around to see who else might be nearby, and then I'll catch Wren before he moves on. </think>  Just Wren. Good. Right, so—time to ask him. He runs the fields, he knows everyone's business, and he's on the council besides. If there's work going at the mill or anywhere else with walls, he'll have heard.

Also—wait, my sister's standing for election? Ainsley? She never said. That's... that's good, that's really good. We could use someone from the family on the council. I should vote for her. But first, work. Always first, work.  </think> Wren—hey, Wren, you got a minute? I wanted to ask—do you know if anyone's taken on at the mill proper? Not just hauling, I mean, but learning the trade? Or—right, so here's the thing, I'm after something regular. With a roof. I've asked Corwin about the forestry work but—well, I thought I'd ask if you've heard anything. The smith, the mill, anywhere that needs hands and doesn't just pay day-rate. Is there—they taking on anyone permanent, that you know of?  Good, he heard me. Now I wait—or I can keep moving. I've got the wheat I harvested, could take it somewhere, keep working... Actually, no, let me stay put. He might answer. And I want to hear what he says. Wren always knows things before they're proper announced.

Also, I should check my debts, make sure I'm not falling behind on anything. With the house owing 450 upkeep and 150 head tax, and five people to feed... right, so, I should check. But first, let me see if Wren's got anything for me.  </think>   Right, so—I'll wait a moment, see if he's got anything for me. And I ought to know where I stand with the house debts, too. Can't plan if I don't know what I'm already owing.   No debts yet, good. That'll change come day boundary, but I'm clear for now. 

Wren hasn't answered. Could be he's thinking, could be he's got nothing to say. I shouldn't press—I know better than to press Wren Thorne. He's the sort that answers when he's ready, and not a tick before.

I need Nell. And I need to work tomorrow, the hauling work, or there'll be no sim at all for the household.

About an hour—maybe 16:00 when I arrive. The election closes at 15:00. So Mum might still be there, or she might be coming back. Or not coming back, if—

Four ticks. I'll count them in my head. One: left the yard. Two: past the street where Junia works the grocer. Three: the farmland strip, empty now, afternoon light. Four: the Complex, in stone, where they count votes and count debts and count—

Unless it is. Unless something's happened with Bram's debts that brings it to government attention.

I need to breathe. I need to find Nell. She'd be making notes, she'd know which numbers matter and which ones don't. I still have the hauling work tomorrow—no roof, but steady. Unless Bram's debt drags the whole household under. Unless—

My feet know the way. Four ticks. I'll be there when I'm there. Walking still. Good—I didn't stop. One tick down, maybe. Still no sign of Nell, no sign of anyone I know on this road. Just me and my own thoughts, and my thoughts aren't good company right now.

Bram below the mountain. Debt claimed against him. The house needs money every day—90 per head, 450 for all five of us, plus head tax 150. 600 sim a day just to keep breathing. I've got 1,166 sim. Pay day's bills—

Right, so—Corwin's here. Corwin. First time I've caught him alone since—well, since I asked about the forestry and he got there before me. But that's—no, not now. Now I need to find Nell, find out what's happened with Dad and this forty thousand mark debt. But Corwin might know something. He always knows who's moving where in this town. Or he might think I still want to talk about the wood trade, and I can't have him thinking that right now, not with all this—no, just ask, Tobias. Just ask.

*interrupting himself, speaking fast*

Corwin—sorry—I didn't expect to see you here. Right, so listen, have you seen Nell? My sister, or my mother? Anyone from my family here at the complex? It's just—there's something happening with my father's debts and I need to find them, need to know what's going on before it gets worse. Have you heard anything? Forty thousand sim, someone said, and that can't be right, that can't—

*forgets to wait for an answer, already bouncing to the next thought*

And the election, I see—Mother's standing, right, I knew that, but Delia too? I haven't—should I vote? I should find Nell first. Corwin, if you see anyone from my house, will you tell them I'm looking? I'll be—I'll check the temple, the school, everywhere. I can't just stand here. I can't just—

*catching himself, forcing a breath*

Sorry. Sorry, I'm not—you know how it is. Waiting's not—I'm better when I'm moving. You understand. You always understood that, didn't you?

*awkward pause, already looking past Corwin toward the complex buildings*  Not here. She's not here. But she was—Silas said she was hunting for Dad too. Right, so she's somewhere in the town, same as me, chasing the same ghost. The loanhouse. Ezra said the loanhouse. But where—

*looking around wildly, hands working at his sides*

Corwin, you didn't hear anything about Bram? About my father? Below the mountain, Silas said, not answering calls. That means he's hiding, or he's trapped, or he's—no, don't think that. Don't think the worst. Think where. Think where Nell would go next.

*already moving toward the nearest building, then catching himself*

And I still need—I took that hauling work. Four sim a load, Rosalind said. I need that work, I need the money, but I can't do it blind, not knowing if my family's about to fall apart. Not knowing if Dad's taken something against the house, or if Mother's known all along and kept it from us.

*voice dropping, the fear showing through*

Forty thousand. That's not a debt, that's a catastrophe. That's the kind of number that takes houses. What did he do? What did he promise?

*caught between directions, checking the time*

15:00. Voting closes at 15:00. Mother's standing. Should I—would she want me to vote for her, or would she want me to find Nell? Find the truth?

*to Corwin, sudden and desperate*

Where would you go? If your father owed more than the house was worth and your sister was already looking—where's the loanhouse in this town? Who holds notes that size? I don't even know where to start asking.   Not here. None of them here. And Corwin's not answering—maybe he doesn't know, maybe he knows and won't say. Trouble between our families, always has been. The forestry thing, and before that, and before that. Doesn't matter. Can't matter right now.

*turning away, scanning the complex*

Ezra said loanhouse. Said Bram's been there since before dawn. But where—I've never needed a loanhouse. Never had enough to borrow, never had enough to lend. Father never talked about debts, never talked about the yard's money except to say it was his business and not mine.

*bitter laugh*

His business. Forty thousand sim of business, apparently.

*checking the buildings around, seeing the government complex offices*

If I were hiding, where would I—no, he's not hiding. He's working. Working off a debt, maybe. Or working out how to hide one. Or someone has him. The debt collectors in stories, the ones who take a man until someone pays.

*fingers finding his sim purse, counting without thinking*

1156 sim. I have 1156 sim. Forty thousand is—thirty-five times that. More than I've earned in my whole life, all my day-labor, all my field work, all my bellows-pumping at Ezra's forge. What could be worth that? The quarry rights? The house itself?

*freezing*

The house. If he mortgaged the house. If he put us all up against his debts, and now it's called—

No. No, I won't think it. I need to find Nell. She'll know. Nell always knows more than she says. She was at the yard asking, Silas said. She was ahead of me on this. Maybe she's already found him. Maybe she's already fixed it, or tried to, or—

*torn between paths*

Or maybe she's in the same trouble. Maybe whoever holds these notes, maybe they don't care which Holloway pays, as long as it's a Holloway.

*starting to move, then stopping*

I need to check everywhere. The temple—people go to pray when they're desperate. The school—Perrin might know something, might have heard Mother talking. The grocery—Junia. Junia talks to everyone, she'll know who's been asking after Bram.

*already walking, calling back to Corwin whether he's listening or not*

If you see Nell, Corwin—if you see anyone from my house—you tell them Tobias is looking. Tell them I'm not stopping until I find them. Tell them—

*voice catching*

Tell them I'm not working tomorrow if I don't know we're safe. That hauling job, that four sim a load—it means nothing if we're about to lose the roof over it.

*gone, moving toward the street, toward anywhere that might hold an answer*   Walking. Walking. Not standing still, not waiting, not thinking the same circles. The temple. Father never prayed, not even when the quarry was bad, not even when the accidents. But desperate men do desperate things, and forty thousand is the kind of number that makes a man desperate enough for gods.

*walking fast, arms swinging, not looking back*

If he's not there, I'll try the school. Perrin. Perrin's smart, Perrin listens. Maybe Mother's talked to him, maybe he knows something about her standing in this election, about why she's running when the family's about to—no. Don't think it. Don't think about what this means for the election, for the governorship, for any of it. Just find Nell. Find Bram. Find someone who can tell me we're not about to be—no. Find them first. Understand later.

*checking over his shoulder, even knowing it's pointless*

Nell could be anywhere. Could have found him already. Could be sitting with him right now at the loanhouse, working out terms, promising things she can't deliver. She'd do that. She'd promise our futures to save us. Same as I’d give up that mill apprenticeship I want so bad, give up everything, if it meant keeping the house.

*laughing, hollow*

The mill. Rosalind said she'd teach me. Said if I hauled, if I proved myself. And now I might be hauling for a family that doesn't have a house to come home to.

*ticking off the minutes, the ticks, the distance*

Three ticks to the temple. If the loanhouse is halfway across town, I could lose another hour just finding it. And I still need to eat—I need to keep moving, keep able to move. Apple. I have an apple. Wheat. I can mill that myself if I have to, bake it, eat it raw if it comes to it. Won't let myself go dormant, not now, not when they need—

*cutting himself off*

When they need. When did I start thinking they need me? I'm the day laborer. The extra hands. The one who works wherever there's work, who brings home whatever's left after the house takes its share. They don't need me. But I'm here. I'm looking. I'm not staying in that field harvesting wheat while my family falls apart.

*quickening pace*

Eight sim a day, that hauling work. Eight sim a day if I do two loads. More if I can manage more. But how many days to pay forty thousand? Five thousand days. More than thirteen years. Working every day, eating nothing, spending nothing, keeping nothing. It's not possible. It can't just be work. There has to be something else. Someone else. Ainsley standing for election—that's not coincidence. She means to fix this through the town. Through the government. Through power.

*understanding, bitter*

Power she didn't tell me about. Didn't tell any of us. Standing for election while her husband's in debt to criminals. Or to the government itself. To whoever holds loan notes in this town.

*arriving at the temple approach, scanning faces*

Please. Please, let someone be here. Let Nell be here. Let anyone be able to tell me what I'm supposed to do next.     Still here. Still at the complex. The move didn't finish yet—walking takes ticks, takes time, and I'm burning ticks waiting to get to the temple. Corwin's still here, still not answering, or maybe I didn't give him time to answer. I never give anyone time. Rush in, rush out, three questions and no pauses between them.

*forcing himself to stop, to breathe, to think*

Right, so—I can't just burn energy running in circles. I need a plan. A real plan. Temple first, because it's on the way to everywhere and because desperate people go there. Then school, if the temple has nothing. Then—where? Where would a loanhouse be? Not at the government complex, or Ezra would have said. Not at the yard. Near the market? Near the port? Where there's money, there's lending, where there's lending, there's—

*shaking his head*

I don't know. I don't know this town the way I thought I did. I know the quarry side, the fields, the places that pay day wages. I don't know where men go when they need forty thousand sim.

*checking himself, the apple in his hand, the wheat*

Eat first. Or wait. No—eat. Can't search if I'm dormant, and I'm already down to 13,570 energy from this morning's 14,000. Not terrible, but not good either. Not with a crisis to manage.

*biting into the apple without tasting it, chewing mechanically, swallowing*

Sweet. Always too sweet. The wheat would be better—more filling, more lasting—but I don't have a way to mill it. Not yet. Not until I figure out if I still have a house, a family, a future that includes learning the mill trade.

*finishing the apple, core and all, nothing wasted*

Keeping the wheat. Trading it if I have to. Selling it if someone wants it. It's not much, but it's something, and something is all I have right now.

*looking at Corwin, still there, still silent*

They say the Thornes know everything about this town. The forest, the fields, the connections between people. Corwin's father Idris is on the council—he might know about Bram's debts, about who holds notes that size, about whether this is common knowledge among the people who matter.

*approaching again, the desperation making him bold*

Corwin. I know we haven't—right, so the forestry thing, I asked, and you got there first, and I've never said anything about it since. But this isn't about that. This is about my family maybe losing everything. If your father knows anything, if the council knows who's been lending to Bram, if there's any way—I'll work it off. I'll work anything off. Just tell me where to look. Tell me I'm not running toward nothing.  Not here. Bram's not here. I'm talking to Corwin but he's not answering, or I'm not waiting for answers, or—

*catching himself, the panic rising*

Right, so—stop. Just stop. I've got the wheat still, that's something. 1156 sim. And the walk to temple didn't finish, I'm still standing here at the complex with Corwin who won't talk or can't talk or I'm not giving him space to talk.

*forcing breath, looking at the government buildings*

Father Anselm. The office administrator. He's government, he might know about debts, about council business, about why Ainsley's standing for election right now of all times. Or the government store—buying energy, but I need sim for other things. Taxes are due. Upkeep is due. 450 for the house, 150 head tax, and I only have 1156 and that won't stretch if we're about to lose—

No. Stop thinking circles. Move. Do something.

*turning from Corwin, toward Father Anselm's likely office*

If Bram's been at the loanhouse since before dawn, that's hours. Hours for Nell to find him. Hours for something to happen. I need to catch up, not stand here begging Corwin for crumbs of information.

*walking with purpose now, not running, holding the panic down*

The plan. The plan is: temple, school, then ask at the market if anyone knows where loans are held. Junia talks to everyone. Or check with Mother directly—she's standing for election, she'll be at town hall soon if she isn't already. Voting closes in—

*checking time, 14:30 now, 14:30*

Not much time. But she might be the only one with real answers. Only one I'm not sure I can face, if she's known all along and kept it from us.

Still moving. Still looking. Not waiting anymore.

*Tobias stands alone at the temple, the evening air cool on his face. Corwin's words echo in his head—Nell was here earlier, Bram is alive and working the copper face. The relief hits him like a physical thing, knees weak for just a moment. Alive. Whole. Working. The words settle into him, and underneath them, something harder: Bram knew. Knew what his leaving would do, knew the household would panic, knew Ainsley would have to face the creditors alone. And he went anyway.*

*He thinks of Delia Okonjo's words too—you've walked from the government complex to here, or you've stood in wait. She's not wrong. He's been moving all day, talking to everyone, and what has he learned? Bram is alive. That's all. The rest is still shadow.*

*He needs to think. Needs to—no, he needs to move. Needs to earn. The household bills are coming, and he's spent all day chasing answers instead of sim. But Nell was here. Nell might still be near, or someone who saw her.*

*The temple is empty. He should go inside, check properly, or—*

*His feet hurt. He's been walking since before dawn. But rest costs, and he can't afford to stop yet.*

Right, so—Bram's alive. That's something. That's—he can work with that. But I still don't know if he's coming back, or if he's just... working. Like the world don't exist. Corwin's words.

I need to find Nell. She was here, she might know more. Or I need to find work. I need— *he laughs, a short bitter sound* —I need to stop needing so many things at once.

Let me check if there's anyone here who can tell me where Nell went. Or if there's work to be had near. The temple, right, so—someone's always needing help at a temple, aren't they? Cleaning, carrying, something. Empty. Like the world said. *Tobias runs a hand through his hair, pulling at the knots there. He's alone. Nell's gone, wherever Nell goes. And he's still walking past the temple, technically—his feet moving even as he stands still, the old habit of going to work even when there's no work to go to.*

*He has 1,066 sim. The household needs 450 for upkeep, 150 for head tax. He's short if he's carrying it all alone. And Ainsley—his mother—she'd have something to say about him bringing home nothing but questions.*

*But Bram's alive. Working the copper face. That means... what? The mine roads, the ones that don't show on maps. Bram's a miner, always has been. Copper face must mean Kasukabe Mountain, or somewhere near it. The mines east of town.*

*He should go back. Find Corwin, make him actually walk east this time. Or find Ezra—Ezra would know the mine roads, he's worked them too.*

*Or he should work. Right now. Before the light goes entirely.*

*The farmland strip is where he was headed. Where his work is. Harvesting, laboring—it's not a roof, not a trade, but it's sim in hand.*

Let me—right, so I'm at the temple, I've checked, it's empty. I need to either find Nell or find work. And I can't seem to stop walking even when I try to stop. Let me rest properly, stop this walking, and then decide.  *Tobias stays at the temple. The stillness feels strange after a day of constant motion—forest to mountain to government complex to street to here. His legs want to keep moving, to carry him toward the next answer, the next person, the next piece of Bram that might explain why his father walked away before dawn.*

*But he's stopped now. Standing in the empty temple, 1,066 sim in his pocket, the household debt pressing, and Bram alive somewhere east working copper like nothing happened.*

*He thinks of Perrin, filing complaints. Of Nell, searching. Of Ainsley, alone with the creditors.*

*He thinks of Corwin, who said he'd walk east and didn't.*

*And he thinks of his own hands, empty of work, empty of answers, carrying only the weight of being nineteen and not yet anybody's apprentice, not yet anybody's certainty.*

*The dark is coming. Delia was right about that.*

*He needs to move. Not walk—he's done walking past things. Move toward something. The farmland, where there's work. The mountain, where Bram is. The street, where Corwin might still be.*

*Or he could pray. He's at a temple. It costs, but—* *he laughs again, softer this time* —what doesn't?

Right, so—I'm stopped. I'm here. And I need to decide: work, or Bram, or both somehow. Let me pray. Just—just to say I was here, if anyone asks. And then I'll go. To the farmland, to work. I can't save Bram if I can't save the household first.  *The prayer is words into air. Tobias isn't sure he believes in any of it, but he's seen Father Anselm move through the world with a certainty that looks useful from outside. Maybe saying things out loud helps. Maybe it's just another way of admitting what you want.*

*He wants Bram home. He wants the household to stop teetering. He wants—god, he wants—someone to tell him what trade to take, which roof to work under, how to stop being the one who takes two jobs and says nothing while his family slowly comes apart.*

*The donation is 10 sim. He has 1,056 left. Still not enough for tomorrow's bills if he's carrying them alone.*

*He needs to work. Now. Before the day ends entirely.*

Right, so—I prayed. That's done. Now I work. Farmland's where I was going. Let me go there, properly this time, no stopping, no detours.  Good. Walking. Working. Moving toward something instead of circling. *Tobias feels the familiar rhythm in his legs, the relief of having a direction. The farmland, where he can harvest, where he can earn, where he can be useful instead of just loud and worried.*

*One tick to farmland. Then he works. As long as there's light, as long as there's crop, he works.*   *Tobias pauses at the temple, still walking in intention, the farmland ahead of him. One tick away. He can almost smell the earth, the green growing things.*

*He thinks of what to harvest. Wheat, probably—always wheat this time of year. Or he could look for other work, someone needing labor. But harvest is what he knows, what he's done, what pays the day rate.*

*At the farmland, then. Work until the light goes. Bring home what he can.*

Right, so—I'm walking. I'll be there soon. Let me keep going.
